=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): opposite (clear paired sets of leaves visible at each node along the stem, with nodes clearly visible in close-up images)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): distal (leaves are spaced along the stem with noticeable gaps between nodes, not densely packed)
B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): simple (each leaf blade is a single, undivided unit; no leaflets present)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): N/A
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): N/A
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): N/A
C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth and continuous, no teeth or serrations visible)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): elliptic (leaf blades are broadest near the middle, tapering gradually to both apex and base)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tip is sharply pointed but not drawn out into a long tail)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): cuneate (base tapers to a narrow point, forming an acute angle with the petiole)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (primary vein runs from base to apex, with secondary veins branching off and running parallel to each other toward the margin)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, closely spaced, numerous (secondary veins are clearly visible, forming a dense network; multiple veins per side of midrib)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (surface has a glossy, reflective quality, especially under light)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or fuzzy structures on leaf surface; surface appears smooth)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petioles are relatively short, supporting leaves close to the stem)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petioles are round in cross-section, without wings or grooves)
D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): woody (stem appears firm and slightly woody, with visible nodes and internodes; not soft or herbaceous)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs on stem surface; smooth texture)
    19. Stem color: brownish-red (stem has a reddish-brown hue, visible in close-up images)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (surface appears smooth without ridges or prominent lenticels)
E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipule structures visible at leaf bases; nodes appear clean)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no exudate visible when stems or leaves are broken; no signs of latex)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no swollen joint or pulvinus visible at leaf base; not applicable as leaf complexity is simple)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): absent (no tendrils observed; all structures are leaves or stems)
F. Notes: Some leaves show light speckling, possibly due to environmental dust or minor surface deposits, not consistent with damage. Minor holes are visible on a few leaves, but no clear pattern or extensive damage. The seedling is growing on a forest floor covered with dry leaf litter. All images show the same individual from multiple angles, confirming consistent morphology. No flowers or fruits are visible.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Locating an individual
Cantarrana, around the station.
Distribution
From Mexico to Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid wet forests on both slopes; 0-1,150 m.
Habit
Tree, 10-35 m tall.
Trunk
Cylindrical trunk, with slender, cylindrical, grayish twigs; small stipules attached to the petiole.
Bark
With smooth, grayish bark.
Leaves
Simple, alternate leaves, 2.5-12 x 0.8-5 cm, ovate to oblong, acuminate apex, rounded to cupped base, whitish or grayish on the underside, 5-9 pairs of secondary veins, entire margin; petioles 3-7 mm long.
Flowers
Greenish-yellow flowers, 1.5 mm long, with absent petals and 3-5 stamens. Inflorescences panicles, up to 16 cm long.
Fruits
Fruits drupes, 1.5-1.8 cm long, pear-shaped to ovoid, pink when ripe.
Diagnosis
Distinguished by its clearly bicolored leaves, the underside whitish to grayish and the thin blade with very fine reticulation. Also, by its pear-shaped fruits.
Habitat
Generally observed in forests on rolling terrain.
Phenology
Fruits observed in July.

Shrub or tree, 2-7(-20) m, the twigs grayish brown; stipules 0.2-0.25 cm. Opposite leaves, petiole 0.2-0.9 cm; blade to [unclear reference], scattered-1% [unclear reference]. Inflorescences with peduncle 0.4-8 cm, [unclear reference], [unclear reference]. Flowers with the articulated pedicel 1/7-1/2 of the base; sepals 1/3-1/2 the [unclear reference] coacuminate at the apex, 1-5-nerved; petals [unclear reference], extended laterally and apical-pubescent on the coast (especially distally); stamens [unclear reference], sparsely puberulent [unclear reference] (> the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.75-2 mm. Fruits [unclear reference]; seeds 6-8 mm, puberulent. Very humid forest, often near water, 0-850 m; [unclear reference] of Agulcahs Pitilla and Talamanca, San Carlos Plains and [unclear reference]. Fl. mar.-may., nov.

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Tree, 4.5-35 m, the young twigs minutely adpressed-pubescent to glabrescent. Leaves with the petiole 0.5-1.2 cm; blade 10-30 X 3.5-12 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, acute to obtuse or (rarely) subtruncate at the base, glabrous on the underside, without domatia or (rarely) with countable trichomes in the axils of the main veins, with (4)5-8 secondary veins on each side. Inflorescences [of Nectandra purpurea] 10-17 cm. Flowers with the tepals (1—)1.2—2(—2.4) mm. Fruits 1-1.5 cm, ellipsoidal; cup ca. 0.3 cm. Very wet and pluvial forest, 0-1550 m; Caribbean [vertical] Cords. of Guanacaste, Triarán and Central (E.B. La Selva), San Carlos and Tortuguero Plains, Low Talamanca, both [vertical] Cord. de Talamanca, [Pacific] vertical, S Coastal Range (Fila Cruces). Flowers [of Nectandra purpurea] May-Sept. [in Nicaragua, Bolivia] and [Venezuela], [in the] Guiana [region], [in] Brazil. (Grayum et al. 8898, MO) Nectandra purpurea is recognized by its leaf blades that dry relatively opaque on the adaxial side, with the secondary veins slightly elevated and interconnected, forming a submarginal vein and by its flowers with the tepals densely covered by brown or yellowish trichomes and (usually) with the staminodes conspicuously elevated. The cupules that dry light brown, ± puberulent, are also distinctive.

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Shrubs or trees, sometimes scandent, monoecious or dioecious, with dotted glands in all their parts and with a strong lemon scent, variably pubescent with simple, fasciculate, or star-shaped to lepidote trichomes; stipules absent. Leaves simple, opposite and decussate, or (sometimes) whorled, entire to denticulate or crenulate to crenate or doubly dentate to serrate (in Costa Rica), pinnately veined, petiolate. Inflorescences axillary (sometimes in leafless nodes), sometimes fasciculate, bisexual or unisexual, cymose. Flowers unisexual, actinomorphic, pedicellate, with a hypanthium (receptacle) obconical to cup-shaped or semi-globose. [The genus Siparuna] is recognized in [Costa Rica] for its shrubby or tree-like habit (sometimes climbing), lack of stipules, simple leaves, opposite or (less frequently) whorled, with translucent glands in all [the genus Siparuna] parts and a strong (and sometimes unpleasant) lemon smell (hence the common name Lr-MONCILLO for all [the species of Siparuna]), unisexual flowers, with stamens and pistils hidden in the hypanthium (receptacle), and aggregate fruits, of drupes sometimes

Tree, ca. 5-30(-40) m. Leaves imparipinnate, 10-30 cm; petiole and rachis generally canaliculate, glabrous or sparsely puberulent; leaflets 5-9, alternate (rarely subopposite), 10-15(-20) X 2.5-4.5 cm, narrowly elliptical or oblong to oblanceolate, attenuated at the base, acute to acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous, generally glabrous, with 13-16 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences axillary, thyrsoid, 10-20 cm, glabrous or puberulent. Flowers with petals white to yellowish-green. Fruits yellow to orange, 1.4-2 X 0.8-1.2 cm, oblong to ellipsoid, densely verrucous (with prominent warts often connected by irregular stripes), often sparsely adpressed-pubescent, with 3 or 4 valves; seeds 1 or 2, black, 0.8-2.2 cm, the aril red. Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the Parque Nacional Carara], [in the Puriscal region (in the Parque Nacional La Cangreja)], [in the Parque Nacional Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica and Panama], [in Ecuador and Peru], [in Northeast Brazil].

Tree, ca. 5-30(-40) m. Leaves imparipinnate, 10-30 cm; petiole and rachis generally canaliculate, glabrous or sparsely puberulent; leaflets 5-9, alternate (rarely subopposite), 10-15(-20) X 2.5-4.5 cm, narrowly elliptical or oblong to oblanceolate, attenuated at the base, acute to acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous, generally glabrous, with 13-16 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences axillary, thyrsoid, 10-20 cm, glabrous or puberulent. Flowers with petals white to yellowish-green. Fruits yellow to orange, 1.4-2 X 0.8-1.2 cm, oblong to ellipsoid, densely verrucous (with prominent warts often connected by irregular stripes), often sparsely adpressed-pubescent, with 3 or 4 valves; seeds 1 or 2, black, 0.8-2.2 cm, the aril red. Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the National Park Carara], [in the Puriscal region] (P.N. La Cangreja), [in the National Park Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica] and [in Panama], [in Ecuador] and [in Peru], [in Northern Brazil]. Trichilia tuberculata is distinguished by its densely verrucous fruits and restricted distribution in [Costa Rica] to very humid forest of the Pacific slope.

Locating an individual
Central Road (CC) 1300 m, Left.
Distribution
From Honduras to Bolivia, Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in mainly very humid climates on both slopes, 10-1,300 m.
Habit
Tree, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion, short branches; glabrous twigs; stipules absent.
Bark
Reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion.
Leaves
Compound odd-pinnate leaves, alternate, leaflets 5-13, 7.5-23 x 2.5-11.2 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, apex short-acuminate, base asymmetric, opposite, glabrous or slightly pubescent on the underside near the central vein, margin entire; petiole 4-20 cm long.
Flowers
Flowers (unisexual) white to yellowish-green and cream; sepals 5, 0.4-0.9 mm long; petals 5, 1.4-2.2 mm long; stamens (8-) 10, unequal, staminodes present in pistillate flowers. The inflorescences have a broad subterminal panicle, with many flowers, 10-35 cm long, rusty-puberulent.
Fruits
Fruit a drupe, 1-1.8 x 0.8-1.3 cm, ovoid, oblong or obovoid, exocarp dark purple to black, endocarp cartilaginous.
Seeds
Seed 1.
Diagnosis
Characterized by its compound leaves, leaflets with entire margins, asymmetric at the base and secondary veins weakly forming a submarginal vein (brochidodromous venation), young leaves with silky pubescence on the underside. Its vegetative appearance and trunk color, as well as its inner bark, resemble or may confuse it with a species of Trichilia (Meliaceae), hence its vernacular names. In mature trees, when making a cut on the trunk, it secretes a slight milky sap in the cambium area.
Habitat
In the rainforest, both in primary forest and secondary vegetation.
Phenology
Flowers observed in May, fruits in October.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Shrub or tree, 1-10(-18) m, the twigs brown; stipules deciduous (but sometimes present with submature leaves). Leaves opposite or with a cuspidate apex, often puberulent and (often) entire or serrated (with the glands of the teeth). Petiole 0.2-0.4 cm, lamina 3.5-11 cm, also hirsute on the midrib on the underside. Flowers with the pedicel articulated at the base; sepals 1/4-1/3 the length of the petals, acute to rounded at the apex, indistinctly 1-3-nerved; petals whitish to pale yellow or orange, 3.5-4.2 mm, glabrous or glabrate; stamens with the connective scale extended laterally and apically (< the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.252 mm. Fruits 1.5-1.9 cm, slightly velvety; seeds 4-8 mm, glabrous. Wet and very wet forest, 0-600+ m; Caribbean slope and near the Continental Divide, Cordilleras of Guanacaste and Talamanca, Plains of Los Guatusos, Tortuguero, and Santa Clara, Lower Talamanca, Pacific slope N Cord. of Talamanca (Cerro Nara), S Nicoya Peninsula, P.N. Carara, Puriscal region (P.N. La Cangreja), vicinity of Palmar Norte, Gulf Dulce region, Burica Peninsula. Fl. Jan., Mar.—May, Jul., Nov. SE Hond.—Pan. [The fruits with the pedicel articulated at the base and glabrous seeds] easily distinguish Rinorea squamata from its congeners in Costa Rica with opposite leaves. Due to its densely puberulent leaf blades and (often) also hirsute on the midrib on the underside, Rinorea squamata is somewhat similar to Rinorea sylvatica, but vegetatively very different due to its smaller stipules and blades with the glands of the acicular teeth (vs. broadly conical).

Shrub or tree, 1-10(-18) m, the twigs brown; stipules deciduous (but sometimes present with submature leaves). Leaves opposite or with a cuspidate apex, often puberulent and (often) entire or serrated (with the glands of the teeth). Petiole 0.2-0.4 cm, lamina 3.5-11 cm, also hirsute on the midrib on the underside. Flowers with the pedicel articulated at the base; sepals 1/4-1/3 the length of the petals, acute to rounded at the apex, indistinctly 1-3-nerved; petals whitish to pale yellow or orange, 3.5-4.2 mm, glabrous or glabrate; stamens with the connective scale extended laterally and apically (< the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.252 mm. Fl. Jan., Mar.—May, Jul., Nov. Southeastern Honduras—Panama.
